extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students in algebraic geometry; readers of Ravi Vakil's 'The Rising Sea' (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and exercises about closed embeddings/closed subschemes, locally-closed embeddings, closed subschemes in projective geometry, and the scheme-theoretic image of a morphism; includes conditions for gluing ideals and computing scheme-theoretic images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: closed embedding / closed immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a closed embedding (or closed immersion) if it is an affine morphism, and for every affine open subset Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) ≅ Spec A, the map B → A is surjective (i.e., of the form B → B/I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the local model Spec B/I → Spec B. Note: the distinction between a closed embedding and a closed subscheme (or between embedding and subscheme) is often blurred in practice. Exercise 8.1.A: a closed embedding identifies the topological space of X with a closed subset of Y, but the closed subset does not determine the closed subscheme (nonreduced/fuzzy information can be lost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embedding gives ideal sheaf on target
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed embedding π : X → Y determines an ideal sheaf I_{X/Y} on Y, namely the kernel of O_Y → π_* O_X; this is a sheaf of ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On each affine open Spec B ⊂ Y one gets an ideal I(B) ⊂ B and the cokernel of I → O_Y is O_X. The I(B) across affine opens give the data of the closed subscheme. Exercises (8.1.E–H) investigate recovering X from these ideals and when the I(B) determine a closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for ideals on affines to define a closed subscheme (gluing condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Y and for each affine open Spec B of Y an ideal I(B) ⊂ B, these data arise from a unique closed subscheme X ⊂ Y if for every affine open Spec B and every f ∈ B the restriction map induces an isomorphism I(B)_f ≅ I(B_f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.1.H states this as a sufficient criterion; three constructive approaches (gluing closed subschemes, defining a sheaf of ideals, or defining X as a closed subset with compatible stalks) are suggested. This condition is what allows the local closed embeddings Spec B/I(B) to glue to a global closed embedding X → Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embeddings are finite (hence of finite type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed embeddings are finite morphisms, and therefore are of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy exercise (8.1.B). Use the affine local description (B → B/I) to check finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of closed embeddings is a closed embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: If X → Y and Y → Z are closed embeddings then the composition X → Z is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy exercise (8.1.C). This follows from the local surjectivity condition on affines and properties of ideals under composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property of being a closed embedding is affine-local on the target
rubrics_metrics.description: The property 'π is a closed embedding' can be checked on an affine open cover of the target Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.1.D: the definition itself is given by an affine-local condition (surjectivity on rings on each affine open).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing scheme V(s) (scheme cut out by a global section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given s ∈ Γ(O_Y), define the closed scheme V(s) as the scheme-theoretic zero locus of s: on each affine Spec B take Spec B/(s_B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.1.I: show this glues to a closed subscheme using Exercise 8.1.H. Properties: if u is invertible then V(s) = V(su); extend to a set S of functions to define V(S). This is the scheme-theoretic analogue of set-theoretic vanishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection of closed subschemes (scheme-theoretic union)
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed subschemes corresponding (affinely) to ideals I1 and I2, the scheme-theoretic union corresponds to I1 ∩ I2 (not I1 I2), while intersections correspond to sums/other constructions as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.1.J(a) discusses unions/intersections; the union must satisfy idempotency property (union with itself = itself), leading to I1 ∩ I2. Exercise 8.1.J(b–d) ask to compute scheme-theoretic intersections and unions in examples, showing how multiplicities/nonreduced structure appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally closed embedding / immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a locally closed embedding (immersion) if π factors as X → Z → Y where the first map is a closed embedding and the second is an open embedding; equivalently X is an open subscheme of a closed subscheme (or a closed subscheme of an open subscheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'immersion' is used in literature but can be ambiguous; Warning: differential-geometric 'immersion' differs. Exercises (8.1.M, 8.1.N) explore equivalences between formulations and show that locally closed embeddings are locally of finite type and stable under composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally closed embeddings are locally of finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: Every locally closed embedding is locally of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy exercise 8.1.L; follows from factorization into closed (finite) followed by open (locally of finite type) maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of several formulations of 'locally closed'
rubrics_metrics.description: Three conditions for V → X are: (i) V is intersection of an open subscheme and a closed subscheme, (ii) V is an open subscheme of a closed subscheme (open followed by closed), (iii) V is a closed subscheme of an open subscheme. (i) and (ii) are equivalent and imply (iii); (iii) need not imply (i)/(ii) in pathological cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.1.M: prove equivalences and examine pathologies (ref: Stacks, tag 01QW). The hint suggests interpreting these as partial commutative diagrams of embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes in projective space via homogeneous polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Any homogeneous polynomial f in x0,...,xn defines a closed subscheme of P^n_A; on Ui it is V(f(x0/i,...,xn/i)) and these local descriptions agree up to multiplication by a unit (power of coordinate). A collection of homogeneous polynomials cuts out a closed subscheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.2.1 and 8.2.C: conversely, closed subschemes of Proj of a finitely generated graded algebra are cut out by homogeneous ideals. Hypersurfaces are closed subschemes cut out by a single homogeneous equation; degree is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear spaces in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear space of dimension n in P^N is a closed subscheme cut out by N−n k-linearly independent homogeneous linear polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.2.D and 8.2.3 give the projective linear subspace construction; linear maps on vector spaces induce closed embeddings of projective spaces (Exercise 8.2.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj of graded ring generated in degree 1 embeds in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: If S• is a finitely generated graded ring generated in degree 1 by n+1 elements, then Proj S• can be described as a closed subscheme of P^n_A via the surjection A[t0,...,tn] → S• and quotient by a homogeneous ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 8.2.G: this is analogous to choosing coordinates in the affine case; combining with other exercises removes the degree-1 generation hypothesis in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite (or projective) morphisms have closed (set-theoretic) image
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is finite (or projective), then the set-theoretic image π(X) is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 8.2.5: the proof uses projectivity of X over an affine base and the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory (7.4.7). Later results show scheme-theoretic image underlying set equals closure of set-theoretic image under reasonable hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : X → Y, the scheme-theoretic image is the smallest closed subscheme Z ⊂ Y such that the composition I_{Z/Y} → O_Y → π_* O_X is zero; equivalently, on affines it is cut out by functions which pull back to 0 on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 8.3.2 and examples: scheme-theoretic image may retain nonreduced 'fuzz' coming from the source. It is the intersection of all closed subschemes containing the image. Examples illustrate when the underlying set differs from the set-theoretic image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples showing scheme-theoretic image behavior (nonreducedness and pathologies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: (1) Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → A^1 via x ↦ ε has scheme-theoretic image Spec k[x]/(x^2) (nonreduced); (2) Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → A^1 via x ↦ 0 has reduced scheme-theoretic image; (3) Spec k[t,t^{-1}] → A^1 via u ↦ t has scheme-theoretic image equal to A^1 though set-theoretic image is A^1 \u007b0; (4) pathological example where scheme-theoretic image is all of Y while set-theoretic image is a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These demonstrate that scheme-theoretic image can be larger and/or nonreduced; Exercise 8.3.3 and Figure 8.4 discuss the pathologies and motivate hypotheses to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local computation criterion for scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: On an affine open Spec B ⊂ Y, define I(B) := ker(B → Γ(Spec B, π_* O_X)). If for each B and g ∈ B the natural map I(B)_g → I(B_g) is an isomorphism, then the I(B) glue and define the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 8.3.3 explains that the question boils down to: given r/g^n vanishing on π^{-1}(D(g)), is there m with r g^m pulling back to 0 on π^{-1}(Spec B)? Three situations guarantee yes: (i) π^{-1}(Spec B) reduced (take m=1), (ii) π^{-1}(Spec B) affine (use algebra of Ag'), (ii') π^{-1}(Spec B) quasicompact (finite affine cover, take max m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 8.3.4: conditions for affine-local computability of scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a morphism and either X is reduced or π is quasicompact, then the scheme-theoretic image of π may be computed affine-locally: on Spec A ⊂ Y it is cut out by the functions that pull back to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents pathologies like Example 4 (Section 8.3.2). Use the affine-local kernel construction I(B) and the previous local-vanishing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 8.3.5: underlying set of scheme-theoretic image equals closure of set-theoretic image under hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.3.4 (X reduced or π quasicompact), the closure of the set-theoretic image of π is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: the set-theoretic image lies in the scheme-theoretic image; the latter is closed. Conversely, on the complement of the closure the preimage is empty and local computation shows scheme-theoretic image is empty there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective and affine cone constructions (Proj/Spec relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Proj S• is a projective scheme, the affine cone is Spec S• and there is a natural morphism Spec S• \ V(S_+) → Proj S•; the projective cone is Proj S•[T] which contains Proj S• (T=0) and whose complement D(T) is isomorphic to Spec S•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 8.2.12–8.2.13 and Exercises 8.2.O–Q explain how Proj and Spec visualize cones and how projective completion adds 'points at infinity'. These constructions are used to understand embeddings and images in projective geometry.
